mappings.note: Naming the mosquito host of the malarial protozoan links the disease to the agent that carries it, the relate-to-cause outcome. Not LO-2, because the pupil is not sorting microorganisms into useful and harmful.

Yeast raising dough is the textbook useful microorganism, so the useful/harmful classification fits. Not LO-5, which is used here for the fermentation process itself rather than for naming the organism.
How malaria spreads ties a phenomenon to its vector, matching LO-4. Not LO-12, because no preventive action is being taken, only the route of spread named.
Recognising Paramecium from its slipper shape is differentiation of organisms by structure. Not LO-2, reserved here for sorting microorganisms as useful or harmful rather than by body form.
Lactobacillus curdling milk is a useful microorganism in food-making. Not LO-4, since nothing harmful is being traced to a cause.

Who first observed bacteria is a story of scientific discovery, the only outcome in the frame that covers the history of science. Not LO-8, which requires the pupil to prepare and describe slides themselves.

How viruses reproduce, only inside a host cell, is a process to be explained. Not LO-1, because the item describes the mechanism rather than asking the pupil to tell viruses apart from other microbes.

Sorting microorganisms that live singly from those that live in colonies is classification by a characteristic. Not LO-1, because no structural feature distinguishes them here, only their mode of living.
Naming the sugar-to-alcohol conversion as fermentation is the explanation of a process. Not LO-2, which is used for the organism behind it rather than the change itself.
The pasteurisation temperature is a practical food-safety technique used in daily life. Not LO-11, because the item asks the working detail, not the story of Pasteur.
Rhizobium in root nodules is the canonical useful microorganism. Not LO-4, because the nitrogen benefit is not a disease cause being traced.
Atmospheric nitrogen being turned into proteins is a step of the nitrogen cycle to be explained. Not LO-13, which would fit a decision about fertiliser use rather than the biochemistry.

The 78 per cent figure is the starting point of the nitrogen-cycle explanation this chapter builds. No classification or causal outcome fits a bare composition fact, and LO-5 is the nearest honest home.
Identifying a chemical preservative is applied food science in the kitchen. Not LO-2, because preservatives are not organisms being sorted.
Hepatitis-A travelling through water relates a disease to its route of transmission. Not LO-12, since no precaution is being chosen, only the route identified.
The general mechanism by which communicable diseases pass between people is a cause-and-route explanation. Not LO-2: diseases, not organisms, are the subject.

Placing viruses in the group with both living and non-living characters is classification by characteristics. Not LO-1, because the item names a whole group rather than distinguishing two named organisms.
Fermentation as the yeast process yielding alcohol and carbon dioxide is a process explanation. Not LO-3, because nothing is being investigated experimentally.
Plasmodium as the cause of malaria is the disease-to-agent link. Kept distinct from the host item, which names the carrier rather than the pathogen, though both sit on LO-4.
Blue-green algae used as biofertiliser is a useful microorganism. Not LO-13, because the item names the organism rather than asking for restrained fertiliser use.
Tuberculosis traced to a bacterium is a disease-to-cause link. Not LO-12, which is used for the BCG prevention item instead.
Knowing what BCG protects against is applying science to health decisions in daily life. Deliberately different from the TB-causation item, which asks for the pathogen rather than the protection.
Cholera traced to its bacterial cause is another disease-to-agent link. Not LO-2, because the options are causes, not organisms to be sorted by usefulness.
Picking the air-borne disease relates an illness to how it reaches a host. Not LO-2, since diseases rather than organisms are being grouped.
Polluted air causing illness is the pollutant-to-effect link that LO-4 names explicitly with smog. Not LO-13, because no protective measure is being proposed.
Yeast used in producing bread and alcohol is the useful-microorganism classification. Not LO-5, used here for the fermentation change itself.
Alcohol produced with the help of yeast identifies a useful microorganism. Not LO-5, because the organism rather than the process is asked for.
Selecting the protozoan disease links an illness to the kind of organism causing it. Not LO-2, since diseases are the options.
Selecting the bacterial disease is the same disease-to-agent link for a different microbe group. Not LO-1, because nothing is distinguished by structure.
Naming the nitrogen-fixing root-nodule bacteria identifies a useful microorganism. Not LO-5, which fits the nitrogen-cycle process rather than the organism's name.
Stopping mosquito breeding to control dengue is a precaution taken in daily life. Not LO-4, because the item asks what to do rather than what causes the disease.
A duplicate of the yeast-and-alcohol item; the useful-microorganism classification applies for the same reason. Not LO-5, the organism being asked for rather than the change.
Recognising an antipyretic among medicines is applying science to everyday health decisions. Not LO-2, because medicines are not organisms and the chapter's point is their correct use.
Yeast raising dough identifies a useful microorganism. Shares the code with its duplicates for the same reason.
Placing algae as producers in the aquatic food chain classifies an organism by its role. Not LO-4, because no phenomenon is being traced to a cause.
Calling rod-shaped bacteria bacilli differentiates organisms by their structure, which is LO-1. Not LO-2, reserved here for the useful/harmful sorting the outcome names.
The bacterium in pea root nodules is the useful microorganism Rhizobium. Not LO-1, because the item asks which organism, not how it is built.
Picking the chlorophyll-bearing microorganism differentiates organisms by a structural and functional property. Not LO-2, since no usefulness judgement is involved.
The protozoan disease item is another disease-to-agent link. Not LO-2, because diseases are the options rather than organisms.
Excluding the organism that cannot fix nitrogen sorts microbes by a function, which LO-1 names directly. Not LO-5, because the nitrogen-fixing process itself is not being explained.
